findings.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via dynamic import of user-controlled filename
findings.description: The `getHandler` function in `src/entry/utils.ts` performs a dynamic `import(filename)` where `filename` is provided by the main process through inter-thread communication. Since the main thread takes this filename from user-provided input, an attacker can supply an arbitrary path to execute local code.
steps_to_exploit: Call `tinypool.run` with a `filename` pointing to a malicious local script
The worker thread receives the message and executes `getHandler` with the malicious path
The `import(filename)` statement triggers the execution of the attacker's code
findings.impact: Remote code execution within the context of the worker thread process.

findings.title: Insecure ESLint configuration disables critical security checks
findings.description: The `eslint.config.js` file explicitly disables multiple `typescript-eslint` rules meant to catch unsafe code execution patterns, such as `no-unsafe-assignment` and `no-unsafe-member-access`.
steps_to_exploit: Developer introduces unsafe data into the codebase
The linter ignores the vulnerability because the rules are set to 'off'
Unsafe code propagates into the production binary
findings.impact: Increases the probability of introducing vulnerabilities like prototype pollution or injection in the codebase.

findings.title: Use of 'eval'-like constructor for import
findings.description: The `getImportESM` function uses `new Function` to return an `import()` call, which is a common technique to bypass transpiler restrictions but effectively acts as an evaluation of string-based code.
steps_to_exploit: Identify an injection point that influences the logic surrounding the dynamic import
The `new Function` context executes with the authority of the worker process
findings.impact: Code injection risks that bypass static analysis tools and environment security constraints.

findings.title: Worker Process Isolation Bypass via `isolateWorkers: false`
findings.description: By default, workers may not be strictly isolated, allowing multiple tasks to potentially share state or exploit memory corruption across tasks if they run in the same process.
steps_to_exploit: Execute a malicious task that alters global state
Execute a subsequent task on the same worker
The second task interacts with the tainted global state
findings.impact: Cross-task data leakage or persistent state attacks.

findings.title: Lack of Input Sanitization for Task Function Names
findings.description: The `getHandler` function expects a `name` parameter to resolve an export. This name is used in a member access chain `(handler as any)[name]`, which is vulnerable to prototype pollution.
steps_to_exploit: Pass `constructor` or `__proto__` as the `name` argument to `runTask`
The `getHandler` function tries to access `handler['constructor']` or `handler['__proto__']`
The system behavior is altered due to access of prototype properties
findings.impact: Prototype pollution resulting in privilege escalation or DoS.

findings.title: Exposure of sensitive environment variables to child processes
findings.description: The `ProcessWorker` spawns new processes using `fork`, which by default copies the current process's environment variables to the child unless carefully filtered.
steps_to_exploit: The main process has sensitive environment variables (API keys, secrets)
A child worker is spawned
The child worker logs or sends these environment variables to an external entity
findings.impact: Leakage of sensitive secrets to potentially untrusted child-process workers.

findings.title: Unchecked Error Serialization leading to info disclosure
findings.description: The `serializeError` function blindly copies all properties of an `Error` object using `...error`. If a custom Error object contains sensitive internal data, that data is serialized and sent to the parent process.
steps_to_exploit: A task throws an Error object with custom properties containing PII
The serialized object is sent to the main process via `postMessage`
The main process logs the object, exposing the PII
findings.impact: Leakage of sensitive data present in error objects.

findings.title: Race condition in `Atomics` state management
findings.description: The `atomicsWaitLoop` relies on `Atomics.load` and `Atomics.wait`. If the timing between reading the count and waiting is misaligned, messages could be processed out of order or dropped.
steps_to_exploit: Send multiple high-frequency messages to a worker
The worker loop enters `Atomics.wait` while a message is already in the pipe
The worker stalls until the next update to the shared buffer
findings.impact: Denial of service (task execution stall) or inconsistent state.

findings.title: Over-privileged File Access in `src/index.ts`
findings.description: The main process reads the project's `package.json` to get the version, exposing the internal directory structure and build metadata.
steps_to_exploit: The worker calls `Tinypool.version`
The code reads `../package.json` relative to the current file path
This confirms directory traversal and file reading capabilities in the main thread
findings.impact: Information disclosure of server-side file structure.

findings.title: Insecure default configuration for worker runtime
findings.description: The `ThreadWorker` does not enforce strict security policies on the created `Worker` instance, relying on default Node.js behavior which may not be hardened for dynamic task execution.
steps_to_exploit: Initialize a `Tinypool` without explicit security hardening options
The worker executes tasks in a relatively permissive sandbox
findings.impact: Reduced security boundary between task code and the host system.

findings.title: Use of `SIGKILL` for forceful termination
findings.description: When a worker fails to terminate gracefully within the timeout, `SIGKILL` is sent, which is non-catchable and can leave resources in an inconsistent state.
steps_to_exploit: Trigger a task that requires cleanup (e.g. file lock)
Initiate termination of the worker
The worker is killed via `SIGKILL` before cleaning up its resources
findings.impact: Inconsistent system state, potential file system corruption, or orphaned handles.

findings.title: Unsafe `process.nextTick` usage for error propagation
findings.description: When a task fails to initialize, the error is thrown inside `process.nextTick`. This can bypass standard `try-catch` blocks and lead to an unhandled exception that crashes the entire application.
steps_to_exploit: Cause an error during task bootstrap
The code executes `throwInNextTick`
The error reaches the top-level process loop, potentially killing the main application
findings.impact: Denial of service through process crash.

findings.title: Lack of resource limiting for task queue
findings.description: By default, `maxQueue` can be set to `Infinity`, which allows an attacker to flood the pool with tasks and consume memory until the process runs out of heap space.
steps_to_exploit: Set `maxQueue` to `Infinity` in configuration
Spam the pool with thousands of large tasks
The memory consumption increases until the event loop blocks or memory limit is hit
findings.impact: Denial of Service due to memory exhaustion.

findings.title: Global state pollution in `process.__tinypool_state__`
findings.description: The pool stores internal flags in the global `process` object. This is a shared namespace and can be modified by any task running in the same process, causing unpredictable pool behavior.
steps_to_exploit: A task modifies `process.__tinypool_state__`
The internal pool logic reads the corrupted `workerId` or `isTinypoolWorker` flag
The pool logic fails to handle tasks correctly, leading to logic flaws
findings.impact: Security bypass or incorrect authorization if pool logic relies on these flags.

findings.title: Incomplete sanitization of worker environment
findings.description: The `initialize` method for `ProcessWorker` merges user-provided environment variables directly into the child process environment, potentially overriding critical system variables.
steps_to_exploit: Provide malicious environment variables (e.g., `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD`) in the `env` config
The worker is spawned with these variables
The worker executes code with modified environment behavior
findings.impact: Environment variable injection into child workers.
